acceptance.output_evidence: The reading, in three answers. (1) NEITHER a naming bug NOR an undocumented decision: the grammar was written down three times -- a PRD, an Andrew-ratified retention policy and the Terraform that justifies versioning-off -- and then not implemented. That is worse than either, because every reader who checks the DESIGN finds the right answer and every reader who checks the WORLD finds the wrong one, and neither has any reason to look at the other. The general form: a spec that is never exercised against its producer is not a control, it is a description. (2) An unversioned bucket holding an archive IS defensible, but only under the premise the Terraform states -- if every write lands on a unique key, the key space IS the version space. The design was sound; the antecedent was never true. An unversioned bucket whose keys are reused is not a weaker archive, it is not an archive at all: it is a cache with an archive's file names, and the file names are what everyone reads. A reader who fetches the key and gets bytes cannot tell a successful retrieval of the cited object from a successful retrieval of a different object with the same name -- BOTH RETURN 200, which is exactly the substrate-card row that asks whether a failure is distinguishable from a genuine negative. (3) The estate already answers the citation question for git and does not know it: rule 22's 'a citation without a vintage is not a citation' with file:line @ commit-ish. There is no S3 equivalent, and 85 undecidable citations in one project's record is what that gap costs. Require bucket/key@ETag for a mutable object, and bare bucket/key ONLY where the record is explicitly naming a POINTER rather than bytes -- the ETag costs nothing, is checkable by anyone later with one head-object, and fails LOUD. With the converse in the same rule: an ETag written beside a citation whose bytes are already gone is a fabricated vintage that reads exactly like a measured one, so the 85 stay undecidable and a record that repaired them would be worse than one that counts them. One caution against over-reading the cell: a citation grammar makes movement VISIBLE, which is strictly weaker than movement not happening.
